subject: Clarification of dynR's capabilities for accurate representation in our manuscript

messages.author: 2f6cb5ca051e8798
messages.subject: Clarification of dynR's capabilities for accurate representation in our manuscript
parts:
Dear dynR development team,

 

I hope this message finds you well. My name is Kenneth Koslowski, and I am part of a research team at Leipzig University currently developing an R package called mlts, which focuses on the estimation of multilevel latent time series models.

 

In the manuscript accompanying our package, we include a section situating mlts among existing R packages for dynamic modeling. In particular, we briefly discuss dynR and ctsem as the two R packages most closely related to the modeling framework we address.

Here is the current draft of the relevant passage:

 

“While there is a myriad of R packages for the estimation of time series models, only a few cover multilevel models suitable for ILD (i.e., longitudinal data from several subjects) or allow for the inclusion of a measurement model. R packages which provide implementations for estimating models akin to models from the DSEM framework are up to date the R packages dynR and ctsem. The dynR package (Ou et al., 2019) provides functions for estimating linear and nonlinear discrete- and continuous-time models with regime-switching properties, including measurement models. However, inter-individual differences in dynamic parameters are not estimated as random parameters in a multilevel model.”

 

Before finalizing the manuscript, we would like to ensure that our description of dynR’s capabilities is both accurate and fair. Could you kindly confirm whether the above characterization correctly reflects the current scope of dynR, particularly regarding the estimation of random effects or inter-individual differences in dynamic parameters?

 

We would greatly appreciate your feedback or any suggested clarifications.

 

With kind regards,

Kenneth Koslowski
Leipzig University

------

Kenneth Koslowski (M.Sc.)

messages.author: b340ad0edf51ca14
messages.subject: Re: [dynr] Clarification of dynR's capabilities for accurate representation in our manuscript
parts:
Hi Kenneth,

Thanks for checking about this!  Broadly speaking, I'd say your description is not accurate.  The main inaccuracy regards ignoring that state space models can extend their latent state to include random effects.  There are limits to the number and kind of random effects that can be incorporated this way, but it works for a wide array of cases.  Below is an incomplete further list of software and methods for multivariate time series with multiple individuals that allow for inter-individual differences.

Lu Ou paper in BJMSP on random effects continuous time models in dynr (2023, DOI: 10.1111/bmsp.12318)

Haya Fatimah has another paper that uses random effects for a nonlinear time series model in dynr (2025, DOI: 10.1037/abn0000960)

Siwei Liu paper in MBR on mixture effects across people in dynr (2020, DOI: 10.1080/00273171.2020.1794775)

Discrete and continuous time, linear dynamic models including measurement models in OpenMx (Hunter, 2018, DOI: 10.1080/10705511.2017.1369354).  Random effects by extending the latent state similar to Ou et al. (2023).

"Random intercepts" state space models in paper by Fei Gu (2014, DOI: 10.1080/00273171.2013.866537)

Doing mixtures in discrete time state space models in discrete time (Hunter, 2024, DOI: 10.1080/00273171.2023.2261224).  Continuous time should work the same, but not paper on it.

Guangjian Zhang's DyFa software recently added some random effects (2025, DOI: 10.1037/met0000722)

Conor Dolan's mkfm6 software can do discrete time state space models with random effects by extended the latent state (Dolan, 2005).

There's not a paper I can point to but OpenMx can also use "definition variables" to estimate person-specific parameters for multi-subject state space models in discrete or continuous time.  See Hunter et al. (2025, DOI: 10.1017/psy.2025.19) for more information on and history of definition variables.

Jonathan Park uses model search to selectively estimate person-specific parameters, extending GIMME to continuous time (2025, DOI: 10.1080/10705511.2024.2429544).

Zach Fisher has been using regularization to estimate person-specific parameters in multi-subject time series (2025, DOI: 10.1080/00273171.2023.2283837)

Cheers,
Mike
